content: Rotavirus infection is the most prevalent nosocomial viral infection in neonates. It represents a significant global health concern. Epidemics involving newer P(6)G9 strains have been documented in neonatal units worldwide. These strains are capable of causing severe symptoms in the majority of infected infants. Consequently, infection control measures become essential, leading to increased utilization of hospital resources. Local mucosal immunity in the intestinal tract plays a critical role in resolving rotavirus infections and providing protection against subsequent infections. Enhancing this local immunity through the oral administration of anti-rotaviral immunoglobulin preparations may represent a promising therapeutic approach, particularly for low birth weight infants. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of oral immunoglobulin preparations in treating rotavirus diarrhea in hospitalized low birth weight infants, defined as those with a birth weight of less than 2500 grams. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of electronic databases was conducted, including The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and Biological Abstracts (BIOSIS). Additionally, the Science Citation Index was used to identify all articles referencing Barnes 1982. Proceedings from the Pediatric Academic Societies, available online at 'Abstracts Online,' were reviewed. Ongoing registered trials were identified through platforms such as www.clinicaltrials.gov and www.controlled-trials.com. Prominent authors in the field were contacted to obtain unpublished articles or additional information on published studies. Reference lists of identified clinical trials and personal files were also examined. The search was updated in July 2011. The inclusion criteria for studies were as follows: 1) Study design: randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials. 2) Population: hospitalized low birth weight infants diagnosed with rotavirus diarrhea. 3) Intervention: oral immunoglobulin preparations compared to placebo or no intervention. 4) Outcomes: at least one of the following outcomes had to be reported—overall mortality during hospital stay, mortality specifically due to rotavirus infection during hospital stay, duration of diarrhea, need for rehydration, duration of viral shedding, duration of infection control measures, length of hospital stay, recurrent diarrhea, or chronic diarrhea. Two independent reviewers were tasked with extracting data from eligible trials. However, no data were available for analysis as no eligible randomized controlled trials were identified. The main findings of this review revealed that no randomized controlled trials assessing the effectiveness or safety of oral immunoglobulin preparations for the treatment of rotavirus diarrhea in hospitalized low birth weight infants were found. The authors concluded that there is a lack of clinical trials addressing the use of oral immunoglobulin preparations for the treatment of rotavirus infections in this vulnerable population. Further research in the form of well-designed clinical trials is necessary to evaluate the potential benefits and safety of this intervention.
